```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.6)
```

`quant2qual` turns behavioral numbers into the kind of prose found in a clinical
or UX case study. It does this in three steps, each a function you can run and
inspect on its own:

1. **Classify** -- `identify_archetype()` places every case on three behavioral
   dimensions and matches it to an archetype.
2. **Narrate** -- `generate_narrative()` writes a case study for a chosen case;
   `generate_cohort_narrative()` writes the cohort synthesis.
3. **Report** -- `write_behavioral_report()` compiles both into Markdown,
   R Markdown, Quarto, HTML or a Neudata-styled PDF.

Everything is rule-based and runs locally: no API, no model, and the same data
always produce the same text.

```{r setup}
library(quant2qual)
```

## The three dimensions

Every domain is described on the same three axes:

| Dimension | Measures | UX example | Learning example | Survey example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **velocity** | time invested | session minutes | time on task | completion time |
| **intensity** | volume of activity | clicks | learning activities | open-text words |
| **friction** | signs of difficulty | errors | failed attempts | quality flags |

## Data

`mock_behavioral_data()` simulates a cohort from a known mixture of signatures,
which makes it useful for learning the package and for checking that the
classifier recovers what was planted.

```{r data}
users <- mock_behavioral_data(200)
users
```

## Step 1: classify

```{r classify}
profile <- identify_archetype(users)
profile
```

Each case gains standardised scores (`z_*`), percentile ranks (`pct_*`), a band
for each dimension (`level_*`), the assigned `archetype`, a `confidence` and the
closest competing archetype (`runner_up`). `summary()` describes the archetypes:

```{r summary}
summary(profile)
```

```{r map, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of standardised session duration against interaction volume, coloured by archetype."}
plot_archetype_map(profile, highlight = 104)
```

The dashed lines are the band edges the classifier used. The tile chart shows
the empirical signature of each archetype, which is the quickest way to check
that the rules carve the data into groups that really differ:

```{r signatures, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Tile chart of mean standardised scores by archetype and dimension."}
plot_archetype_signatures(profile)
```

## Step 2: narrate

```{r narrative}
generate_narrative(profile, id = 104)
```

Three registers are available. `"ux"` drops the statistics and ends in
recommended actions; `"brief"` gives one paragraph:

```{r brief}
generate_narrative(profile, id = 104, style = "brief")
```

`select_cases()` picks exemplars so you do not have to: the clearest example of
each archetype by default, or the most extreme, or the most borderline.

```{r select}
ids <- select_cases(profile)
ids
generate_narrative(profile, ids[1:2], style = "ux")
```

The cohort synthesis describes the whole distribution: who dominates, how much
of the cohort is friction-led, how concentrated friction is, how the
dimensions relate and how cleanly the cohort was classified.

```{r cohort}
generate_cohort_narrative(profile)
```

```{r case-plot, fig.height = 2.6, fig.alt = "Dot plot of one case's standardised scores over the cohort's box plots."}
plot_case_profile(profile, 104)
```

## Step 3: report

```{r report}
md <- write_behavioral_report(profile, style = "brief")
cat(substr(md, 1, 900))
```

The same report renders to PDF in the Neudata house style (this needs pandoc
and a LaTeX installation such as TinyTeX):

```{r pdf, eval = FALSE}
write_behavioral_report(
  profile,
  file = "behavioral-report.pdf",
  format = "pdf",
  title = "Checkout usability study",
  client = "Example Ltd",
  confidentiality = "Confidential"
)
```
